title: Examining the Potential Role of Respect in Health Disparities
abstract: ABSTRACT The social factor thought to be at the heart of health disparities is social devaluation that disadvantages members of certain groups. Respect is arguably the opposite of devaluation and as such may counteract social processes of devaluation that contribute to health disparities. We define respect and discuss its behavioral correlates and social function. We review the very limited direct data on whether (dis)respect is associated with physical health. We then identify candidate mechanisms that may help explain how intergroup and interpersonal experiences of respect get under the skin to influence health and conclude with discussion of whether respect may play a role in explaining racial and socioeconomic health disparities in the United States. Respect is central to models of intergroup relations, and there is very preliminary evidence that respect, when examined on its own rather than as part of another construct such as discrimination, is associated with physical health outcomes such as self‐rated health, mortality, and cardiovascular disease. Inconsistent associations also arise in this literature, such as interpersonal respect being more commonly reported among Black and lower SES individuals in the US if measured in daily life, but showing expected associations when measured at the intergroup‐level or as a one‐time self‐report. Thus, while there is logical and empirical reason to believe that respect may be good for our health, much less is known about who experiences respect, from whom, and with what consequences for racial and socioeconomic disparities in physical health in the US.
